CausalChain: Chronic liver injury and inflammation → recruitment and polarization of tumor‐associated macrophages (TAMs) with high TGF‐β signaling → establishment of an immunosuppressive microenvironment that impairs effector T-cell function → targeted delivery of CRISPR/Cas9 via ligand-decorated nanoparticles to knock down TGF‐β receptors in TAMs → reprogramming TAMs from an M2 (suppressive) to an M1 (pro‐inflammatory) phenotype → enhanced antigen presentation and effector T-cell activation → improved efficacy of conventional immunotherapies (eg, checkpoint inhibitors and CAR-T cells) in HCC.
Hypothesis: Targeted CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of TGF-β signaling in tumor-associated macrophages, delivered via hepatocyte/tumor-targeting nanoparticles, can reprogram the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in hepatocellular carcinoma and synergize with immunotherapies to improve antitumor efficacy.
Abstract: This review synthesizes emerging data on gene‐based, viral‐vector and non‐viral nanoparticle approaches, oncolytic viruses, CRISPR/Cas9, and immunotherapeutic strategies including immune checkpoint blockade and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T‐cell therapy in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). We propose a novel strategy that leverages targeted CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing delivered by ligand‐decorated nanoparticles to reprogram the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) of HCC by disrupting TGF‐β signaling in tumor‐associated macrophages. By diminishing TGF‐β–mediated immune suppression, the edited macrophages may shift toward a pro‐inflammatory, M1‐like phenotype, ultimately enhancing the recruitment and effectiveness of effector T cells and improving the therapeutic response to subsequent immunotherapies (eg, checkpoint inhibitors or CAR‐T cells). This combined approach promises synergistic antitumor activity and offers a testable route toward overcoming immunoresistance in advanced HCC.
